title: I Tried Grindr’s New Experience, Edge, and It Actually Changed How I’m Dating
summary: Grindr's sex and relationships expert Zachary Zane puts Edge to the test, discovering how gAI™ helps cut through the noise, spark better conversations, and lead to more IRL meet-ups.
body_markdown:
“Is it me?”


No matter how hard we try not to ask ourselves that question when a guy doesn’t respond on Grindr, many of us spiral into negative talk. If I were more muscular, twinkier, hairless, hairier, had a fatter ass, a bigger dick, or a more symmetrical face, *then* I’d get his attention. The truth is, yeah, maybe if you had a certain attribute he found arousing, that would get his attention, but it might not. He might just not be a guy who responds to messages, or you two simply aren’t compatible.


And wouldn’t it be nice to know that? Specifically, to know before messaging a stranger on Grindr how likely he is to respond, or whether you'll connect and share the same sexual and platonic interests?


Grindr’s newest subscription experience, Edge, uses gAI™ to help users increase the likelihood of connecting with someone that you’re actually compatible with. Don’t get me wrong, I was *extremely* skeptical at first. For one, like, do we really *need* this? Isn’t Grindr already pretty damn good at connecting people with shared, how do I put this euphemistically, *proclivities?*


Two, as a writer, I’ve been extremely hesitant to adopt AI features because it steals from creatives and artists. It’s why I still pay illustrators cold, hard cash, commissioning them for an illustration on my[Substack, BOYSLUT zine](https://zacharyzane.substack.com/) . Would it be easier, cheaper, and faster to get an AI illustration? Of course, but I’m trying to be ethical here.


That said, this is different. gAI™ is not “stealing” from anyone. Edge uses gAI™ to make Grindr more personal by drawing on signals like profile information, tags, who you’ve replied to, who you’ve ignored, and how you engage with other profiles. It’s not taking content from other people or “stealing” from anyone. If you don’t want to share your info, you can opt out in your settings. (Still, sensitive health information, including HIV status and testing details, is[never used in AI](https://www.grindr.com/blog/youre-in-control-of-your-gai-experience) .)


So, I spent the next three months testing the Edge feature out during its beta phase. And you know what? I get it.


At first, I didn’t change who I messaged, even if Edge said we were not likely to click. I figured, what the hell, shoot my shot, right? Generally, I feel like that is a good mindset to have, or at least it was a good mindset pre-gAI™. Because I did notice that when the new feature said we likely weren’t a match, well, who would have figured, but he didn’t often respond!


So I changed my behavior. I decided to focus on the men the Edge said I clicked with—my tribes, position, and tags aligning. I ended up sending these men an initial message with more than a “hey.” If Edge predicted we’d click and flagged a response rate over 50%, I actually put some effort into wooing him.


Go figure, it worked! Edge really sets you up for success. If you are likely going to click with a guy and you put in that little extra effort to show you’ve read their profile—making them feel special—I don’t want to say it’s “in the bag,” but chances are really high you two will get along *swimmingly* .


Edge encouraged me to focus and invest in the men who likely want me. Previously, I wasn’t sure who was worth that extra effort. It’s simply impossible to go that extra mile for everyone you message, but now I know. I have fewer convos, more responses, and, notably, far more meet-ups. Because at the end of the day, that is my goal. I am not online to chit-chat for days. I want to meet up IRL and have fun. And isn’t that what AI should be doing: facilitating more real-world, in-person connections, not making us feel more disconnected from humanity?


Still, I shoot my shot with the “wildcards”—profiles that are new or somewhat unpredictable in their behavior. You never know, and yes, I get fewer responses from them, but that stings less because I know it’s more of a long shot. I also don’t get my hopes up with them, with Edge helping me manage my expectations.


Navigating rejection and “wasting time” on the app are two of the biggest complaints from users, myself included, and Edge directly addresses both. (Again, what AI, in my opinion, should be doing—addressing problems and not creating more.)


So, is Edge for everyone? If you want to stop guessing, stop wasting time, and start actually meeting up with guys who are as into you as you are into them, then yeah, it’s a total game-changer.


But don’t take my word for it. Upgrade your Grindr experience with Edge, set your intent, and see who’s actually waiting on the other side of the screen. Your next great connection (or incredible night) is closer than you think.
